strengths: The paper identifies a relevant weakness of Gaussian location-scale causal discovery under skewed noise and proposes a natural extension using the skew-normal family.
The methodology is presented clearly, with explicit penalized likelihoods, spline parameterization, optimization details, and an appendix covering identifiability and implementation settings.

Evaluation includes both in-family skew-normal noise and out-of-family generalized-normal noise, numerous established benchmarks, strong baselines, and an ablation showing that ECM refinement materially improves downstream accuracy.

SKEWD-IT is competitive on established benchmarks, while SKEWD-LL performs strongly on the proposed skewed-noise datasets. The work is a useful, albeit specialized, contribution to bivariate causal discovery.
The application has limited direct ethical risk, and the manuscript honestly notes restrictions concerning multivariate extension, heavy tails, and marginal modeling.
weaknesses: The headline evidence is not sufficiently discriminative: the deliberately misspecified IGCI-G baseline obtains essentially perfect accuracy on the proposed skewed datasets. This indicates strong direction-revealing simulation artifacts unrelated to correctly modeling skewness. The paper acknowledges this observation but does not investigate it, use artifact-controlled generators, or report results separately for the mixed skew-normal and generalized-normal mechanisms.

The best-performing SKEWD-LL variant is not generally a valid joint-likelihood comparison. It assigns equal standard-normal marginal scores after standardization, although standardization does not make a variable Gaussian. In the synthetic experiments only the true cause is generated as Gaussian; the effect used as the hypothetical reverse-direction cause is generally non-Gaussian. Proposition 1 assumes normality rather than justifying it, so the perfect SKEWD-LL results may partly reflect a favorable data-generation assumption.

There is a technical inconsistency in the claimed ECM procedure. In CM-step 1, both the updated location coefficients and updated shape parameter are computed using iteration-k quantities; the shape update uses the old location coefficients rather than the newly updated ones. This is neither the stated sequential conditional maximization nor an evident joint maximization, so the asserted monotonicity guarantee does not follow unless the displayed algorithm differs from the implementation.

The empirical study does not evaluate parameter recovery, likelihood convergence, sensitivity to initialization or spline dimensions, runtime, or repeated-run variability despite a highly stochastic and expensive pipeline involving Bayesian optimization and CMA-ES. Dataset-level standard deviations are not substitutes for uncertainty across random seeds.

SKEWD-IT appears to test dependence using residuals from models fitted on the same observations, without sample splitting or cross-fitting. Flexible splines and data-selected penalties can distort residual-independence comparisons, and this issue is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is only partial: many hyperparameters and hardware details are supplied, but random seeds, baseline configurations, runtime, and an accessible code/data location are missing from the provided manuscript. There are also minor presentation errors, including duplicated method names in the ablation discussion, an incorrect figure reference, and inconsistent notation.

The limitations discussion omits important threats exposed by the experiments: hidden confounding, simulation artifacts, likelihood misspecification, optimization failures, and the computational cost. No research-ethics statement is provided; while risk is low, the paper should caution against interpreting observational directions as causal when assumptions such as causal sufficiency fail.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of location-scale causal models: Gaussian or symmetric noise assumptions can be inappropriate when residuals are skewed.

The skew-normal model is a sensible extension that nests the Gaussian case, and the manuscript provides explicit likelihood, spline regularization, latent-variable formulation, and optimization updates.

Evaluation includes both likelihood- and independence-based variants, multiple established baselines, 13 existing benchmarks, synthetic data beyond the fitted skew-normal family, and an ablation of ECM refinement.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with readable figures, detailed appendices, and an honest limitations section. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The likelihood rule is not theoretically justified as a causal score. After standardization, the paper assigns identical standard-normal marginal scores even when the variables are not normally distributed, then compares conditional training likelihoods. Standardization does not imply Gaussianity, and general LSNM identifiability does not establish that the causal direction has the larger conditional likelihood. Thus the perfect SKEWD-LL results do not validate a generally sound decision rule.

Soundness: SKEWD-IT appears to estimate regressions and test residual independence on the same observations. Flexible spline fitting can alter the null distribution of HSIC and induce optimistic or direction-dependent behavior. No sample splitting, cross-fitting, or calibration experiment is reported, while raw HSIC p-values are compared across two fitted models and also treated as confidence scores.

The claimed ECM monotonicity is not adequately supported by the stated algorithm. The displayed lambda update uses the previous psi rather than the newly updated psi, despite the description of sequential conditional maximization, and the rho step is solved heuristically with CMA-ES rather than guaranteed maximization. Convergence, likelihood monotonicity, and sensitivity to random initialization are not empirically checked.

Significance of the evidence is limited. The strongest gains occur on synthetic benchmarks constructed from the same sigmoidal mechanisms and skewness assumptions motivating the method. IGCI-G also obtains essentially perfect accuracy there despite being acknowledged as strongly misspecified, indicating a major benchmark artifact that is noted but not investigated.

On the 13 established benchmarks, ROCHE is better than both SKEWD variants on mean accuracy and AUDRC. SKEWD-LL improves over LOCI-LL by only 0.35 percentage points on mean accuracy and performs poorly on the real-world Tuebingen data (45.97%, versus 77.27% for ROCHE). No paired tests, confidence intervals, repeated-seed analysis, or robustness-to-sample-size study establishes that the small aggregate differences are meaningful.

Originality is modest: the principal method replaces Gaussian noise with a skew-normal family and combines existing CMA-ES, Bayesian optimization, and an adapted published ECM procedure. The paper supplies no new skew-normal-specific identifiability result and largely inherits the causal inference rules from prior work.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although many SKEWD hyperparameters are listed, the promised public implementation URL is absent, important HSIC and baseline configurations are not specified, stochastic variability is not reported, and no runtime comparison is given despite an exceptionally expensive nested optimization procedure involving cross-validation, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and ECM in both directions.

The limitations discussion omits the most consequential issues: validity and calibration of the two directional scores, same-sample residual testing, optimization failures, synthetic-generator bias, sensitivity to tuning and initialization, and computational cost. These unresolved central evidential and methodological weaknesses prevent acceptance despite the useful problem formulation.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript presents a coherent skew-normal location-scale noise model, derives its penalized likelihood and ECM updates, and clearly connects the fitted models to likelihood- and independence-based causal-direction criteria. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/56763bf030ae4f12b8b237adfe86ba35/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Empirical evidence supports the intended narrow claim: SKEWD-LL achieves 100% accuracy on all six proposed skew-noise benchmarks, including generalized-normal noise with skewness 1.750 outside the skew-normal family's attainable range. The ECM ablation is useful, showing gains of up to 12.5 accuracy points for likelihood scoring and 28–34 points for independence testing on heteroscedastic data.

Significance and originality: Explicitly accommodating asymmetric noise addresses a meaningful weakness of existing LSNM estimators. Combining skew-normal conditional models, spline-based location and scale functions, heuristic initialization, and ECM refinement is a useful methodological contribution, even though its individual ingredients are established.

The evaluation covers multiple relevant LSNM baselines and 13 established benchmarks. SKEWD-IT is competitive beyond the targeted skewed setting, reaching 85.02% mean accuracy and ranking second to ROCHE's 87.69% across those benchmarks.

Presentation and reproducibility are generally strong: the paper is well organized, gives equations and algorithmic details, specifies spline dimensions, optimization bounds, stopping rules, cross-validation settings, software/hardware information, and includes exact per-dataset results. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges the bivariate scope, heavy-tailed distributions, and the likelihood variant's marginal-Gaussian assumption. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The likelihood criterion lacks a convincing statistical justification on most evaluated data. Standardization does not make an arbitrary marginal Gaussian; Proposition 1 only applies when the original variable is Gaussian. In a direction comparison, the effect marginal generally is not Gaussian even when the true cause is. Consequently, dropping both marginal likelihoods yields a heuristic conditional score rather than a valid comparison of the stated joint models, weakening the theoretical basis of the paper's best-performing SKEWD-LL variant.

The new synthetic evaluation has a potentially strong generator bias: every cause is Gaussian and the functions come from one sigmoidal family. The nearly perfect performance of the explicitly misspecified IGCI-G baseline, which the authors themselves note, is evidence that these benchmarks contain exploitable regularities beyond skewness. Experiments with diverse or matched cause marginals, non-sigmoidal mechanisms, direction-swapped constructions, and separate results for skew-normal versus generalized-normal noise are needed to isolate the claimed benefit.

The headline perfect results lack uncertainty analysis. Only aggregate accuracies for apparently single generated collections are reported, without repetitions over dataset-generation seeds, confidence intervals, paired tests, or sensitivity to sample size. This makes it difficult to judge whether modest differences on established benchmarks are reliable.

SKEWD-IT compares HSIC p-values after fitting flexible regressions on the same observations. P-values are not calibrated effect-size measures for ranking two directions, and in-sample residual estimation can distort independence tests. Cross-fitting or held-out testing, alongside calibration and type-I-error experiments, would strengthen this part substantially.

The procedure appears computationally heavy: Bayesian optimization evaluates 60 penalty pairs with eight-fold fitting, each involving CMA-ES, followed by two directional ECM refinements. The manuscript reports hardware and iteration limits but no runtimes, convergence/failure rates, seed sensitivity, or computational comparison with baselines. Random seeds are also not specified, which matters for CMA-ES and Bayesian optimization.

The contribution remains limited to bivariate orientation, and the skew-normal family cannot represent heavy tails or absolute skewness above approximately 0.995. The paper acknowledges these scope limitations, but does not discuss other important limitations such as causal sufficiency, selection bias, measurement error, optimization instability, and benchmark bias. Minor presentation errors—including duplicated naming of CMA-ES variants and inconsistent figure references—should also be corrected. Overall, this is a useful and promising contribution, but the scoring justification and evaluation design keep it at weak accept rather than accept.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and underexplored failure mode of location-scale causal discovery: misspecification under skewed noise. Extending Gaussian LSNMs with a skew-normal conditional model is natural and practically useful.

The proposed estimation pipeline is technically substantive, combining penalized GAMs, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES initialization, and ECM refinement. The appendix provides equations, pseudocode, spline dimensions, bounds, stopping criteria, cross-validation settings, and an ablation showing that ECM materially improves accuracy.

The bivariate evaluation is broad. It includes controlled skew-normal and generalized-normal simulations, 13 established benchmarks, numerous relevant baselines, and both likelihood- and independence-based variants. Results convincingly show robustness on the proposed high-skewness benchmarks, including under distributional misspecification beyond the skew-normal family.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. Assumptions, identifiability conditions, computational scaling, Gaussian-marginal dependence, unobserved-confounding risks, and high-stakes misuse are discussed explicitly. The research-ethics discussion is appropriate.
The multivariate extension is a useful proof of concept. Separating performance with an estimated versus oracle Markov equivalence class helps identify the PC stage as an important source of error.
weaknesses: The strongest results come from newly constructed synthetic benchmarks closely aligned with the assumed LSNM and spline model. On the 13 established benchmarks, SKEWD does not establish a clear overall advantage: ROCHE achieves higher mean accuracy and AUDRC than either SKEWD variant. No real dataset isolates a setting with independently justified skewed structural noise, limiting the evidence for the stated real-world motivation.

The likelihood variant is not generally a full likelihood comparison. Standardization makes Gaussian pseudo-marginal scores equal, but it does not make a nonlinear effect marginal Gaussian. Appendix A.3 only justifies asymptotic standard normality when the original variable is Gaussian, whereas the synthetic effects and many benchmark variables need not be. The KDE ablation demonstrates consequential sensitivity to this choice, and no consistency result is given for the resulting conditional-score procedure.

The multivariate evidence is narrow: only sparse synthetic graphs with 6 or 10 nodes, n=1000, one mechanism family, and one noise setting are evaluated. Moreover, the manuscript specifies SN(0,1,0.985), where 0.985 is the shape parameter under its own notation; this corresponds to distributional skewness of only about 0.13, not 0.985. This inconsistency undermines the interpretation of the multivariate study as evidence under strongly skewed noise.

Experimental uncertainty and robustness are insufficiently characterized. There are no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests for accuracy differences, limited analysis across sample sizes or graph densities, and no sensitivity analysis for the PC threshold, spline dimensions, or stochastic optimizer. Standard deviations across heterogeneous benchmark datasets are not substitutes for repeated-run uncertainty.

Computational practicality is unclear. The method combines multi-fold Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES with population 100 and up to 5000 iterations, and up to 5000 ECM iterations, yet reports no runtimes or matched compute comparison. The exponential dependence on unresolved PC edges further limits the multivariate method.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the footnote claiming public code ends without a URL, baseline configurations and random seeds are largely unspecified, and five error-terminated GraN-DAG++ runs are excluded rather than counted as failures or analyzed. These omissions make the reported comparisons difficult to reproduce reliably.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored failure mode: asymmetric noise can misspecify Gaussian location-scale models. The skew-normal formulation is a natural extension that includes the Gaussian case.

The proposed estimator combines flexible spline models for location and scale with penalized likelihood optimization. The manuscript provides derivations, pseudocode, hyperparameter information, and an ablation showing that ECM refinement materially improves over the initial CMA-ES solution.

The bivariate evaluation is fairly broad in number of methods and includes both likelihood- and independence-based variants, 13 established benchmarks, and out-of-model generalized-normal noise whose skewness and kurtosis exceed the skew-normal family.
The multivariate experiment, oracle-MEC diagnostic, and KDE marginal ablation help expose where errors originate rather than reporting only a single headline result.

The paper is generally well organized and readable. It explicitly acknowledges limited scalability, marginal-distribution misspecification, causal sufficiency, and risks from applying causal discovery in high-stakes settings.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that the strongest evidence comes from newly constructed benchmarks closely aligned with the method: causes are Gaussian, mechanisms use the same random sigmoidal family as the fitted model, and part of the noise is exactly skew-normal. SKEWD-LL's perfect accuracy is therefore weak evidence for broad skewness robustness. The fact that the strongly misspecified IGCI-G baseline makes only one error across these six datasets is a major warning that generator artifacts make causal direction unusually easy to identify.

On the 13 established benchmarks, SKEWD does not improve the state of the art: ROCHE achieves 87.69% mean accuracy and 92.90% AUDRC, compared with 85.02% and 91.65% for the better SKEWD variant. SKEWD-LL reaches only 45.97% accuracy on the real-world Tübingen benchmark. Thus the claimed practical reliability is not demonstrated outside the authors' tailored synthetic setting.

The multivariate comparison is not sufficiently controlled. SKEWD first restricts its search using PC and then scores DAGs inside the estimated MEC, whereas the reported baselines solve a less constrained end-to-end graph-learning problem. There is no PC-plus-alternative-orientation or random-orientation baseline to isolate the benefit of the skew-normal score. Evaluation is limited to matched skew-normal mechanisms at d=6 and d=10, and five failed GraN-DAG++ runs are excluded, potentially favoring that baseline rather than addressing robustness fairly.

No uncertainty intervals or paired statistical tests are reported despite 100 generated instances. Dataset-level means also weight heterogeneous benchmarks equally. These omissions make it difficult to judge whether the comparatively small established-benchmark differences are meaningful.

The stated ECM procedure has a technical ambiguity that should be resolved. In CM-step 1, the update for psi uses the old lambda, while the displayed update for lambda uses the old psi rather than the newly updated psi. These parallel updates are not the sequential conditional maximizations ordinarily required by ECM, so the claimed monotonic likelihood improvement does not follow from the algorithm as written.

The likelihood scoring protocol is underspecified: it is not fully clear whether causal scores use training, held-out, penalized, or unpenalized likelihood after cross-validation. Likewise, important baseline settings, PC test levels, random seeds, runtime comparisons, and sensitivity to spline dimension and optimizer initialization are missing. The manuscript claims public code, but the provided artifact contains no usable repository address.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The work adapts an existing skew-normal ECM construction to spline-based location-scale regression and combines it with standard RESIT/likelihood scoring and PC-based MEC enumeration. It provides no new skew-normal-specific identifiability result; the identifiability discussion largely restates prior general LSNM theory, and Proposition 5.1 is a straightforward consequence of fixed parent sets within an MEC.

The limitations discussion is honest about Gaussian marginals, confounding, and scalability, but it does not confront the more consequential benchmark-alignment and comparison-fairness issues. Several presentation errors also remain, including incorrect figure cross-references, a duplicated CMA-ES-LL label where CMA-ES-IT is intended, and inconsistent location/scale terminology. Overall, the idea has merit, but the current evidence does not reliably support the paper's broad robustness and multivariate superiority claims.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/f45ba574a3cf4cbe87ff1ecd28042b58/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} develops a coherent skew-normal LSNM, penalized likelihood, ECM-based refinement, and both independence- and likelihood-based causal scores. The method is connected appropriately to existing LSNM identifiability results.

The evaluation is broad for a primarily bivariate paper: six new skew-noise settings, including generalized-normal noise outside the fitted skew-normal family, 13 established benchmarks, and comparisons with several LSNM and general causal-discovery baselines. SKEWD-LL attains 100% accuracy on all six new settings, while SKEWD-IT remains competitive on established benchmarks.

The ablation directly supports the use of ECM refinement: on skewed LS datasets, it improves independence-based accuracy by roughly 28–34 percentage points and likelihood-based accuracy by as much as 12.5 points over the CMA-ES initialization.

Significance: Robustness to asymmetric noise addresses a plausible and practically relevant misspecification in existing LSNM methods. The method preserves the Gaussian special case and therefore offers a useful extension rather than a narrowly separate model.

Originality: Explicitly integrating skew-normal conditional models, a tailored ECM procedure, and causal-direction scoring for LSNMs is a meaningful methodological contribution, even though its ingredients individually build on established skew-normal regression and causal-discovery ideas.

Presentation is clear and well organized. Assumptions, model construction, optimization, causal scores, identifiability context, and limitations are stated explicitly; the appendix provides derivations, pseudocode, hyperparameters, ablations, and per-dataset results.

The paper treats limitations and ethics appropriately. It acknowledges marginal misspecification, restricted scalability, lack of interaction effects, causal sufficiency, and the danger of harmful interventions following incorrect causal conclusions.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical evidence is partly distribution-matched: the proposed method is tested on data generated with skew-normal noise or closely related controlled skew distributions. Evidence from genuinely skewed real-world causal systems is absent. On the 13 established benchmarks, SKEWD-IT (85.02% accuracy) is below ROCHE (87.69%), while SKEWD-LL reaches only 77.43%, so the claim of broad practical superiority should remain qualified.

The multivariate contribution is only a proof of concept. It is evaluated on sparse, synthetic, skew-normal LSNMs with 6 or 10 nodes, and its near-perfect oracle-MEC results do not account for the substantial errors introduced by estimating the MEC. Exhaustive enumeration within the MEC and exponentially many parent configurations also limit applicability to small graphs.

Statistical uncertainty is insufficiently characterized. The paper reports means and standard deviations across benchmark datasets but no paired significance tests, confidence intervals over generated instances, sensitivity to sample size, or variability across optimization seeds. This matters because CMA-ES and Bayesian optimization are stochastic.

The ECM presentation contains a potentially important ambiguity: the stated update for lambda uses the old psi estimate even though psi is updated in the same conditional-maximization step. As written, this is not clearly a joint or sequential maximization and therefore does not transparently justify the claimed monotonic increase of the penalized likelihood. The indexing or convergence argument should be corrected or clarified.

Likelihood scoring relies on Gaussian marginals after standardization, which standardization does not make Gaussian. The weakness is visible on the Tübingen benchmark, where SKEWD-LL obtains 45.97% accuracy. KDE helps several non-Gaussian benchmarks but substantially harms the proposed skew-noise settings, leaving model selection between marginal estimators unresolved.

Reproducibility is promising but not complete in the supplied manuscript: algorithms and major hyperparameters are detailed and code availability is asserted, yet the displayed public-code location is blank. Runtime, random seeds, baseline-tuning protocols, and the treatment of five error-terminated GraN-DAG++ runs should also be documented more fully, especially given the expensive nested cross-validation, CMA-ES, and ECM pipeline.

The generalized additive multivariate model is additive across parents and cannot represent interactions. Together with causal sufficiency, faithfulness, and the restricted skew-normal conditional family, this considerably narrows the scope of the multivariate claims.
